title: Utility Grid Site Planning Workflow
problem: Utilities and infrastructure planners may need to combine grid demand, siting constraints, zoning, local priorities, and simulation outputs when evaluating locations for new power infrastructure. This can involve repetitive multi-source analysis and decision preparation.
target_buyer: Electric utilities, energy infrastructure planners, engineering firms, municipal energy offices, and project developers
evidence: A public engineering article described a new ORNL algorithm for identifying urban power project sites using 24-hour grid simulations while weighing grid needs, zoning, and local priorities.
The underlying workflow suggests recurring planning friction around gathering, reconciling, and evaluating multiple siting factors before infrastructure decisions are made.
existing_alternatives: Utility planning tools, GIS systems, grid simulation software, consulting services, and specialized siting platforms already exist. The current signal does not establish that JakeAI has a superior optimization algorithm.
identified_gap: Potential workflow gap: automate the collection, normalization, comparison, documentation, and preliminary ranking of siting inputs before expert engineering review, rather than attempting to replace advanced grid simulation or utility planning software.
workflow_description: Collect approved planning inputs, organize grid and siting requirements, gather zoning and public-policy constraints from permitted sources, normalize the information, identify missing inputs, compare candidate locations using user-defined criteria, produce a traceable preliminary ranking, and generate an expert-review packet. The workflow must not claim to perform regulated engineering analysis unless the required models and licensed expertise are actually present.
feasibility_notes: A limited decision-support workflow appears technically feasible using existing data-processing and document-analysis capabilities. Reproducing ORNL's algorithm or performing authoritative grid engineering is outside the scope of this candidate.
risks: Engineering and infrastructure decisions can be safety-critical
Public-source data may be incomplete or outdated
Zoning and regulatory information varies by jurisdiction
The workflow must not be marketed as replacing licensed engineering review
The underlying ORNL research and implementation must not be copied
validation_experiment: Interview or obtain public evidence from utility planners, engineering firms, or infrastructure developers to determine whether preliminary siting-data aggregation and comparison is a recurring pain point. Then prototype a narrow workflow using only public or user-supplied data and test whether it reduces preparation time without making engineering decisions.
